items.summary: This is part 2 of Newslaundry’s investigation into voter deletions in Kichha, Uttarakhand. A BJP booth-level agent filed Form 7 objections that he said were accepted on ECI’s directions. Here, we speak to voters whose names are missing from the final roll. In Sirauli Kalan, a Muslim-dominated urban locality in the Kichha assembly constituency in Uttarakhand, Newslaundry met Kulsum, a 25-year-old mother of two, against whom Rajesh Tiwari, a BJP booth-level agent (BLA), filed a Form 7 objection and whose name was subsequently deleted from the final voter list. She didn’t even know her name had been deleted from the voter list until we met her. Against her name, Tiwari's objection was “Already Enrolled” (in another state as a voter). But the notice she got from the local electoral registration officer (ERO) office stated a different reason. The notice says, “The age gap between you and your parents is more than 50 years, whose details were used to link you to the voter list prepared during the previous SIR, it appears that this has occurred due to incorrect mapping.” After receiving the notice in August, Kulsum submitted her Aadhaar card, a copy of the family register certificate, ration card and details from the 2002-03 voter list. “After submitting these documents, the official told me, ‘Now your name will be corrected in the voter list,’ but my name was deleted anyway,” she said. Kulsum and her mother-in-law Asif, a 34-year-old resident of Kichha, found his name in the draft electoral roll, but it was missing from the final voter list. Asif’s brother, Arif, told Newslaundry , “We received a notice from the ERO, so we submitted our documents. Still, our name is missing from the electoral roll,” he said. The reason stated in the notice, however, was different from the one in Tiwari’s objection. All three were registered at booth number 134 in Kichha. Tiwari was the objector here too. Sahid and his father, Salim, run a small restaurant in Sirauli Kalan. items.title: Uttarakhand ERO refused BJP worker’s bulk Form 7 objections. After ECI complaint, 5,359 were accepted
items.summary: In August, Newslaundry reported how bulk Form 7 applications were being used to target voters in Uttarakhand during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Across constituencies in the state, thousands of Form 7 applications were filed by BJP workers, with most objections targeting Muslim voters. In Kichha constituency of Udham Singh Nagar district, our investigation found that 4,390 names that appeared in the draft electoral roll were missing from the final roll released on October 3. Of these, around 670 were voters against whom Form 7 objections had been filed in August, 509 of them by Rajesh Tiwari, a booth-level agent (BLA) associated with the BJP. Of the 6,884 Form 7 objections accepted in Kichha, 5,359 were Tiwari’s. He is a close associate of former MLA Rajesh Shukla and BJP district cell coordinator of Udham Singh Nagar. Speaking to Newslaundry , Tiwari claimed that the local electoral registration officer (ERO) initially refused to accept the bulk Form 7 objections, saying there was no such provision in Election Commission of India (ECI) rules. He said he then emailed the ECI and complained against the ERO. Newslaundry has not been able to independently verify the contents of this email. “Within two days of sending the email, the ERO’s office called and asked me to submit the objections,” he said, adding that the ERO accepted the bulk Form 7 objections on directions from the ECI. Kichha ERO Gaurav Pandey neither confirmed nor denied these claims. He told Newslaundry , “Our SIR has been completed. We have heard the claims and objections, and that process is also over. Other than that, I cannot comment on this.” Asked whether he had received specific directions from the ECI on Tiwari’s objections, he said, “I cannot comment on this.” He added that the process had taken place two months ago and he could not recall all the details. On the deletions, he said, “Whatever we have done is in accordance with ECI rules and regulations.” Separately, in Uttarakhand, the claims and objections period ended on August 13 and was not extended. According to Form 10 data from the office of the Uttarakhand Chief Electoral Officer (CEO), reviewed by Newslaundry , 504 of Tiwari’s 5,359 accepted Form 7 objections carry an acceptance date of August 14. We have emailed the Uttarakhand CEO and the Kichha ERO asking why these objections were accepted a day after the deadline. We will update this report if we receive a response. items.title: Kerala High Court changes its internship policy; only those in final 2 years of LL.B allowed
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has revised its 2026 internship policy, introducing new rules governing applications, entry passes, attendance and the conduct of law students interning at the High Court. The revised policy, titled ' Internship Policy for the High Court of Kerala-2026 (Amended), ' was notified on October 17 and lays down detailed procedures governing internships at the High Court. Clause 6(a) of the policy states that "o nly students in the last two years of their law courses shall be eligible to undergo an internship in the High Court. " The restriction, however, does not apply to internships permitted at the discretion of judges. The policy applies to law students interning under High Court judges and other sections of the Court as well as offices including those of the Advocate General, Additional Solicitor General, Director General of Prosecution, Deputy Solicitor General, Kerala State Legal Services Authority, Mediation Centre, Bar Council of Kerala and other advocates. For internship opportunities under the judges, applications will be processed only after obtaining their consent. Under the new framework, students will be required to submit their internship applications through an online module, which will be developed by the High Court. Until the module becomes operational, applications and other internship-related procedures will continue to be handled online. The applications are to be forwarded through the principal or head of the institution where the student is studying. The Public Relations Officer (PRO) of the High Court will be responsible for overseeing the internship program, including processing applications and maintaining attendance records. Interns are prohibited from using mobile phones, cameras or recording devices inside courtrooms. Recording court proceedings in any manner or circulating it on social media to compromise the Court's security would lead to immediate termination of the internship, as per the policy. They are also required to maintain confidentiality and avoid disturbing court proceedings. The interns have to record their attendance daily and the actual number of days where they are physically present in the Court would be counted as the internship period for issuance of internship certificates. items.title: Keralam: Local BJP leader admits role in Rs 8 cr robbery of KMCC in Qatar
items.summary: In September this year, a local Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Parappil Balakrishnan, a welder from Kozhikode, surrendered before the police to admit his involvement in an alleged case of theft committed in the office of the Kerala Muslim Cultural Centre (KMCC) in Qatar. His surrender comes nearly a year after the alleged crime, involving five others from Keralam, who are accused of stealing 31 lakh Qatari riyals, which comes to Rs 8.06 crore in Indian rupees. Balakrishnan had posted a video before going to the police, claiming that he was tricked into joining the others with the offer of a welder’s job. He named ‘Bombay Shaji’ as the man who offered the job, and two others, called Rashi and Salih Bavah, who joined him on the flight to Qatar. They had stayed in a three-star hotel there, he said. On September 18, 2025, they went in a car to the office of the KMCC. Balakrishnan said that he didn’t know that was where they were headed, and when he resisted, he was threatened and ordered to use his welding skills to break the locker containing the money. He named a man called ‘Thamar’ as giving orders on the phone. At the Koyilandi Police Station in Kozhikode, where the case was registered last month, Bombay Shaji, Rashi and Salih Bhava were named as the first three accused who allegedly committed the crime with the help of the other three accused - Balakrishnan, Hassan Mammali and Nizar. They are charged under Sections 309(4) (robbery) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). In the last few days, a few audio clips have been circulating in the media, purportedly in the voice of Bombay Shaji, conversing with others involved in the crime. These conversations take the tone of blackmail, suggesting that the crime might have been a 'quotation' or conducted under the instructions of someone who wanted the KMCC office burgled. The KMCC is a welfare organisation for the expatriates from Keralam, affiliated to the Indian Union Muslim League. There was also criticism about the delay in registering the crime. The FIR was filed after Abdul Rahim PK, vice president of the KMCC in Qatar, made the complaint in September 2026. However, PMA Salam, general secretary of the Indian Union Muslim League (IUML) in Keralam, said that if any KMCC members were found to be involved in the crime, strong action would be taken against them. Parappil Balakrishnan was a member of the BJP, and the IUML could not do anything about that, he said.
